claim: Notch signaling dictates cell fate decisions in mammalian cells including megakaryocytes.
source: Notch signaling dictates cell fate decisions in mammalian cells including megakaryocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch signaling's role in cell fate determination.

claim: Notch signaling is induced through binding of five independent ligands (DLL-1, 3, 4 and Jagged-1 and -2) to four isoforms of cognate Notch receptors (Notch1 to Notch4) on surface of adjacent cells.
source: Signaling is induced through binding of five independent ligands, Delta-like ligands (DLL)–1, 3, 4 and Jagged (Jag)–1 and –2 (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009), to four isoforms of cognate Notch receptors, Notch1 to Notch4, on surface of adjacent cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kopan and Ilagan, 2009.

claim: Ligand binding incites sequential α- and γ-secretase-mediated proteolytic events releasing the intracellular domain of Notch receptor (NICD).
source: Binding incites sequential α- and ϒ-secretase-mediated proteolytic events releasing the intracellular domain of Notch receptor (NICD) that initiates downstream effects of Notch activation (Maillard et al., 2003; Blanpain et al., 2006; Qiao and Wong, 2009; Andersson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Maillard et al., 2003; Blanpain et al., 2006; Qiao and Wong, 2009; Andersson et al., 2011).

claim: Platelets are circulating blood cells having central role in hemostasis and pathological thrombus formation.
source: Platelets are circulating blood cells having central role in hemostasis and pathological thrombus formation that can lead to serious vaso-occlusive pathologies like myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about platelet function.

claim: Despite lack of genomic DNA, platelets express several transcription factors.
source: Despite lack of genomic DNA platelets intriguingly express several transcription factors (Spinelli et al., 2010) and developmental morphogens like Wnt (Kumari and Dash, 2013; Steele et al., 2009) and Sonic Hedgehog (Kumari et al., 2014), whose non-canonical non-genomic roles in platelet biology and thrombogenesis remain poorly characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spinelli et al., 2010.

claim: Platelets express developmental morphogens like Wnt and Sonic Hedgehog.
source: Despite lack of genomic DNA platelets intriguingly express several transcription factors (Spinelli et al., 2010) and developmental morphogens like Wnt (Kumari and Dash, 2013; Steele et al., 2009) and Sonic Hedgehog (Kumari et al., 2014), whose non-canonical non-genomic roles in platelet biology and thrombogenesis remain poorly characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Kumari and Dash, 2013; Steele et al., 2009; Kumari et al., 2014).

claim: Notch signaling has been linked to differentiation of megakaryocytes.
source: Notch signaling has been linked to differentiation of megakaryocytes (Sugimoto et al., 2006; Mercher et al., 2008), the platelet precursor cells in bone marrow, though there also have been reports to the contrary (Dorsch et al., 2002; Poirault-Chassac et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Sugimoto et al., 2006; Mercher et al., 2008).

claim: Notch1 and DLL-4, as well as their respective transcripts, are abundantly expressed in human platelets.
source: Here, for the first time, we demonstrate abundant expression of Notch1 and DLL-4, as well as their respective transcripts in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (RT-qPCR, Western blot, flow cytometry).

claim: When platelets were challenged with thrombin, synthesis and surface translocation of Notch1 and DLL-4 were significantly augmented.
source: When platelets were challenged with thrombin, a potent physiological agonist, synthesis and surface translocation of Notch1 and DLL-4 were significantly augmented.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DLL-4 instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: DLL-4 induced P-selectin externalization in human platelets.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: DLL-4 induced release of adenine nucleotides from human platelets.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: DLL-4 induced shedding of extracellular vesicles from human platelets.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: DLL-4 amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome in human platelets.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: DLL-4 induced rise in intracellular calcium in human platelets.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: DLL-4-induced platelet activation was associated with generation of NICD.
source: Interestingly, DLL-4, in turn, instigated activation of human platelets, as evidenced from binding of PAC-1 and fibrinogen to surface integrins αIIbβ3, P-selectin externalization, release of adenine nucleotides, shedding of extracellular vesicles (EVs), amplified tyrosine phosphoproteome and rise in intracellular calcium, associated with generation of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: DLL-4 significantly enhanced phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT in platelets.
source: In parallel DLL-4 significantly enhanced phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Attenuation of γ-secretase significantly abrogated platelet activation responses triggered either by DLL-4 or thrombin.
source: Attenuation of γ-secretase significantly abrogated platelet activation responses triggered either by DLL-4 or thrombin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase significantly impaired arterial thrombosis in mice.
source: Inhibition of γ-secretase, too, significantly impaired arterial thrombosis in mice and platelet thrombus generation ex vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase significantly impaired platelet thrombus generation ex vivo.
source: Inhibition of γ-secretase, too, significantly impaired arterial thrombosis in mice and platelet thrombus generation ex vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Preclusion of DLL-4-Notch1 interaction by pre-incubation with a blocking antibody prohibited thrombin-mediated platelet aggregation.
source: Furthermore, preclusion of DLL-4-Notch1 interaction by pre-incubation with a blocking antibody prohibited thrombin-mediated platelet aggregation and shedding of EVs, which underscores a critical role of Notch signaling in inducing human platelet activation in synergism with physiological agonists in a juxtacrine manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Preclusion of DLL-4-Notch1 interaction by pre-incubation with a blocking antibody prohibited shedding of EVs.
source: Furthermore, preclusion of DLL-4-Notch1 interaction by pre-incubation with a blocking antibody prohibited thrombin-mediated platelet aggregation and shedding of EVs, which underscores a critical role of Notch signaling in inducing human platelet activation in synergism with physiological agonists in a juxtacrine manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The Cq value for NOTCH1 mRNA in platelets was 27.
source: The Cq values for housekeeping genes (GAPDH and ACTB) were determined as 21 and 23, respectively, whereas that for NOTCH1 was 27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, A and B), which was reflective of abundant expression of NOTCH1 mRNA in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NOTCH1 mRNA is abundantly expressed in human platelets.
source: The Cq values for housekeeping genes (GAPDH and ACTB) were determined as 21 and 23, respectively, whereas that for NOTCH1 was 27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, A and B), which was reflective of abundant expression of NOTCH1 mRNA in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cq value data and comparison with housekeeping genes.

claim: NOTCH isoforms 2, 3 and 4 had Cq values greater than 33 in platelets.
source: Contrasting this, NOTCH isoforms 2, 3 and 4 had Cq values greater than 33 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was notable existence of Notch1 peptide in human platelets.
source: Keeping with above, there was notable existence of Notch1 peptide in human platelets, whose level significantly increased upon stimulation with thrombin (1 U/ml), a potent physiological agonist (Figure 1, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Notch1 peptide level significantly increased upon stimulation with thrombin (1 U/ml).
source: Keeping with above, there was notable existence of Notch1 peptide in human platelets, whose level significantly increased upon stimulation with thrombin (1 U/ml), a potent physiological agonist (Figure 1, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with puromycin (10 mM) significantly deterred synthesis of Notch1 peptide.
source: Pre-treatment of platelets with puromycin (10 mM) singnificantly deterred synthesis of this pepetide (Figure 1, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: There was considerable expression of Notch1 on platelet surface membrane.
source: We also observed considerable expression of Notch1 on platelet surface membrane, whose level enhanced significantly (by 65.71%) upon thrombin-stimulation (Figure 1, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Notch1 surface expression enhanced significantly (by 65.71%) upon thrombin-stimulation.
source: We also observed considerable expression of Notch1 on platelet surface membrane, whose level enhanced significantly (by 65.71%) upon thrombin-stimulation (Figure 1, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The Cq of DLL4 in platelets was found to be 26.
source: The Cq of DLL4, JAG1, and JAG2 were found to be 26, 31 and 30, respectively while those for DLL isoforms-1 and -3 were higher than or equal to 33 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), reflective of DLL4 being the most abundantly expressed Notch ligand transcript in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: DLL4 is the most abundantly expressed Notch ligand transcript in human platelets.
source: The Cq of DLL4, JAG1, and JAG2 were found to be 26, 31 and 30, respectively while those for DLL isoforms-1 and -3 were higher than or equal to 33 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), reflective of DLL4 being the most abundantly expressed Notch ligand transcript in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cq values of different Notch ligands.

claim: Platelets express DLL-4 peptide whose level increased significantly when cells were challenged with thrombin (1 U/ml).
source: Consistent with above, platelets were found to express DLL-4 peptide whose level increased significantly when cells were challenged with thrombin (1 U/ml) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Rise in DLL-4 could be averted upon pre-incubation of platelets with puromycin (10 mM).
source: Rise in DLL-4 could be averted upon pre-incubation of platelets with puromycin (10 mM) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Thrombin significantly augmented surface translocation of DLL-4 by 64.31%.
source: Thrombin, too, significantly augmented surface translocation of DLL-4 by 64.31% (Figure 1G and H), thus raising possibility of DLL-4-Ntoch1 interaction on adjacent platelet membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Enucleate platelets have limited capacity for protein synthesis.
source: As enucleate platelets are known to have limited capacity for protein synthesis, the present observations add Notch1 and DLL-4 to the growing list of platelets translatome.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about platelet biology.

claim: Notch1 and DLL-4 are part of the platelet translatome.
source: As enucleate platelets are known to have limited capacity for protein synthesis, the present observations add Notch1 and DLL-4 to the growing list of platelets translatome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing synthesis of Notch1 and DLL-4 in platelets.

claim: Interaction of Notch1 with cognate ligands leads to sequential cleavage of the transmembrane receptor and generation of NICD.
source: Interaction of Notch1 with cognate ligands leads to sequential cleavage of the transmembrane receptor and generation of NICD (Iso et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iso et al., 2003.

claim: Exposure of platelets with DLL-4 (15 µg/ml) for 10 min led to significant rise (by 5.1-fold) in level of NICD.
source: Remarkably, exposure of platelets with DLL-4 (15 µg/ml) for 10 min led to significant rise (by 5.1-fold) in level of NICD (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: NICD generation is mediated through activity of γ-secretase.
source: As NICD generation is mediated through activity of γ-secretase, we next investigated the contribution of this protease in DLL-4-induced NICD release in platelets.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DAPT (10 μM) for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced NICD release (by 25.33%).
source: Pre-treatment of platelets with either DAPT (10 μM) or DBZ (10 µM), specific inhibitors of γ-secretase, for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced NICD release (by 25.33% and 23.77%, respectively) (Figure 2A and B), strongly suggestive of functional DLL-4-Notch1-NICD signaling axis in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DBZ (10 µM) for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced NICD release (by 23.77%).
source: Pre-treatment of platelets with either DAPT (10 μM) or DBZ (10 µM), specific inhibitors of γ-secretase, for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced NICD release (by 25.33% and 23.77%, respectively) (Figure 2A and B), strongly suggestive of functional DLL-4-Notch1-NICD signaling axis in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There is a functional DLL-4-Notch1-NICD signaling axis in human platelets.
source: Pre-treatment of platelets with either DAPT (10 μM) or DBZ (10 µM), specific inhibitors of γ-secretase, for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced NICD release (by 25.33% and 23.77%, respectively) (Figure 2A and B), strongly suggestive of functional DLL-4-Notch1-NICD signaling axis in human platelets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing DLL-4-induced NICD generation that is blocked by γ-secretase inhibitors.

claim: Level of NICD was reduced by 2.4, 43.4, 70.3, and 84.9%, respectively, when platelets were stored for 1, 3, 5, and 8 hr at 37 °C in presence of 1 mM calcium.
source: Interestingly, level of NICD was reduced by 2.4, 43.4, 70.3, and 84.9%, respectively, when platelets were stored for 1, 3, 5, and 8 hr at 37 °C in presence of 1 mM calcium (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NICD level was not considerably affected upon storage of cells at 22 °C.
source: However, NICD level was not considerably affected upon storage of cells at 22 °C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Calpain is activated in platelets stored at 37 °C, and not at 22 °C.
source: As calpain, the Ca2+-dependent thiol protease, is known to be activated in platelets stored at 37 °C, and not at 22 °C (Wadhawan et al., 2004), we pre-incubated cells at 37 °C with either calpeptin (80 µM) or ALLN (50 µM), specific inhibitors of calpain, or divalent ion chelator EGTA (1 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wadhawan et al., 2004.

claim: Pre-incubation with calpain inhibitors or EGTA led to significant recovery of NICD intensity.
source: Significant recovery of NICD intensity under above conditions (Figure 2D) was consistent with NICD being a calpain substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NICD is a calpain substrate.
source: Significant recovery of NICD intensity under above conditions (Figure 2D) was consistent with NICD being a calpain substrate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing recovery of NICD with calpain inhibitors.

claim: Incubation of platelets with calcium ionophore A23187 (1 µM) for 10 min at 37 °C in presence of 1 mM calcium brought about significant reduction (by 29.77%) in the level of NICD.
source: In keeping with this observation, incubation of platelets with calcium ionophore A23187 (1 µM) for 10 min at 37 °C in presence of 1 mM calcium brought about significant reduction (by 29.77%) in the level of NICD, which was restored upon pre-treatment with either of the calpain inhibitors (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A23187-induced reduction in NICD was restored upon pre-treatment with calpain inhibitors.
source: In keeping with this observation, incubation of platelets with calcium ionophore A23187 (1 µM) for 10 min at 37 °C in presence of 1 mM calcium brought about significant reduction (by 29.77%) in the level of NICD, which was restored upon pre-treatment with either of the calpain inhibitors (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Hallmark of activated platelets is the conformational switch of its surface integrins αIIbβ3 that allows high-affinity binding of fibrinogen.
source: Hallmark of activated platelets is the conformational switch of its surface integrins αIIbβ3 that allows high-affinity binding of fibrinogen, associated with release of granule contents, rise in intracellular free calcium and shedding of extracellular vesicles.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about platelet activation.

claim: DLL-4 (15 µg/ml for 10 min at RT) prompted enhanced binding of PAC-1-FITC by 3.07-fold.
source: To study the effect of Notch ligands we pre-incubated platelets with DLL-4 (15 µg/ml for 10 min at RT) that prompted enhanced binding of PAC-1-FITC (that recognizes the open conformation of αIIbβ3) (Figure 3, A and B) and fibrinogen-Alexa Fluor 488 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) by 3.07- and 3.13- folds, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: DLL-4 (15 µg/ml for 10 min at RT) prompted enhanced binding of fibrinogen-Alexa Fluor 488 by 3.13-fold.
source: To study the effect of Notch ligands we pre-incubated platelets with DLL-4 (15 µg/ml for 10 min at RT) that prompted enhanced binding of PAC-1-FITC (that recognizes the open conformation of αIIbβ3) (Figure 3, A and B) and fibrinogen-Alexa Fluor 488 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) by 3.07- and 3.13- folds, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DLL-1 was notably ineffective in eliciting PAC-1 or fibrinogen binding.
source: DLL-1 was notably ineffective in eliciting such response.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Platelets exposed to DLL-4 were found to have significant surface expression of P-selectin.
source: Furthermore, platelets exposed to DLL-4 were found to have significant surface expression of P-selectin as a measure of α-granule secretion while no change was observed with DLL-1 (Figure 3, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: No change in P-selectin expression was observed with DLL-1.
source: Furthermore, platelets exposed to DLL-4 were found to have significant surface expression of P-selectin as a measure of α-granule secretion while no change was observed with DLL-1 (Figure 3, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: DLL-4 induced release of ATP from platelet dense granules.
source: In keeping with above, DLL-4 also induced release of ATP from platelet dense granules (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luminescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DLL-4, on its own, did not incite platelet aggregation at the doses employed.
source: Although DLL-4, on its own, did not incite platelet aggregation at the doses employed, it could significantly potentiate thrombin-mediated platelet aggregation (Figure 4, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by aggregometry data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: DLL-4 could significantly potentiate thrombin-mediated platelet aggregation.
source: Although DLL-4, on its own, did not incite platelet aggregation at the doses employed, it could significantly potentiate thrombin-mediated platelet aggregation (Figure 4, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by aggregometry data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DAPT led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced activation of integrin αIIbβ3.
source: Platelets were pre-treated with DAPT (10 μM), a specific γ-secretase inhibitor, for 10 min at RT followed by exposure to DLL-4. Interestingly, we observed significant drop in DLL-4-induced activation of integrin αIIbβ3 (Figure 3, A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), P-selectin exposure (Figure 3, C and D) and release of ATP from platelet dense granules (Figure 3E) when platelets were pre-incubated with DAPT.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DAPT led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced P-selectin exposure.
source: Platelets were pre-treated with DAPT (10 μM), a specific γ-secretase inhibitor, for 10 min at RT followed by exposure to DLL-4. Interestingly, we observed significant drop in DLL-4-induced activation of integrin αIIbβ3 (Figure 3, A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), P-selectin exposure (Figure 3, C and D) and release of ATP from platelet dense granules (Figure 3E) when platelets were pre-incubated with DAPT.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DAPT led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced release of ATP from platelet dense granules.
source: Platelets were pre-treated with DAPT (10 μM), a specific γ-secretase inhibitor, for 10 min at RT followed by exposure to DLL-4. Interestingly, we observed significant drop in DLL-4-induced activation of integrin αIIbβ3 (Figure 3, A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), P-selectin exposure (Figure 3, C and D) and release of ATP from platelet dense granules (Figure 3E) when platelets were pre-incubated with DAPT.
evidence: This claim is supported by luminescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: P-selectin expressed on stimulated platelets serves as a ligand for P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1) receptor on leukocytes leading to platelet-leukocyte interaction.
source: P-selectin expressed on stimulated platelets serves as a ligand for P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1) receptor on leukocytes leading to platelet-leukocyte interaction.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about platelet-leukocyte interactions.

claim: Addition of DLL-4 (15 µg/ml, 10 min) to fresh human blood led to significant boost in platelet-neutrophil and platelet-monocyte aggregates.
source: Remarkably, addition of DLL-4 (15 µg/ml, 10 min) to fresh human blood led to significant boost in platelet-neutrophil and platelet-monocyte aggregates, which was reduced upon pre-treatment with DAPT (40 µM, 10 min) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DLL-4-induced platelet-leukocyte aggregates were reduced upon pre-treatment with DAPT (40 µM, 10 min).
source: Remarkably, addition of DLL-4 (15 µg/ml, 10 min) to fresh human blood led to significant boost in platelet-neutrophil and platelet-monocyte aggregates, which was reduced upon pre-treatment with DAPT (40 µM, 10 min) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Notch signaling plays a critical role in platelet-leukocyte interaction and thrombogenesis.
source: Above observations underline a critical role of Notch signaling in platelet-leukocyte interaction and thrombogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing DLL-4-induced platelet-leukocyte aggregates that are blocked by DAPT.

claim: Rise in intracellular Ca2+, [Ca2+]i, is a hallmark of stimulated platelets.
source: Rise in intracellular Ca2+, [Ca2+]i, is a hallmark of stimulated platelets (Mallick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mallick et al., 2015.

claim: Exposure to DLL-4 (15 µg/ml) for 10 min evoked significant rise (by 1.34-fold) in [Ca2+]i in Fura-2 AM-stained platelets in presence of 1 mM extracellular Ca2+.
source: Interestingly, exposure to DLL-4 (15 µg/ml) for 10 min evoked significant rise (by 1.34-fold) in [Ca2+]i in Fura-2 AM-stained platelets in presence of 1 mM extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 3, F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium measurement data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Chelation of extracellular calcium led to significant drop in rise in [Ca2+]i (by 64.87%).
source: To validate whether calcium entry from external medium contributed to rise in [Ca2+]i, we pre-treated cells with EGTA (1 mM) followed by incubation with DLL-4. Chelation of extracellular calcium led to significant drop in rise in [Ca2+]i (by 64.87%), suggestive of DLL-4-mediated Ca2+ influx in these platelets (Figure 3, F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium measurement data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: DLL-4 mediates Ca2+ influx in platelets.
source: To validate whether calcium entry from external medium contributed to rise in [Ca2+]i, we pre-treated cells with EGTA (1 mM) followed by incubation with DLL-4. Chelation of extracellular calcium led to significant drop in rise in [Ca2+]i (by 64.87%), suggestive of DLL-4-mediated Ca2+ influx in these platelets (Figure 3, F and G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduction in [Ca2+]i rise with EGTA.

claim: Platelet-derived extracellular vesicles (PEVs) are cellular fragments ranging in size between 0.1 and 1 µm that are shed by activated platelets.
source: Platelet-derived extracellular vesicles (PEVs) are cellular fragments ranging in size between 0.1 and 1 µm that are shed by activated platelets (Kulkarni et al., 2019; Heijnen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kulkarni et al., 2019 and Heijnen et al., 1999.

claim: PEVs are pro-coagulant in nature that significantly contribute to haemostatic responses.
source: PEVs are pro-coagulant in nature that significantly contribute to haemostatic responses (Sinauridze et al., 2007; Mallick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sinauridze et al., 2007 and Mallick et al., 2015.

claim: Exposure of platelets to DLL-4 (15 µg/ml) for 10 min led to extensive shedding of PEVs, which were 4.29-fold higher in count than those released from vehicle-treated counterparts.
source: Exposure of platelets to DLL-4 (15 µg/ml) for 10 min led to extensive shedding of PEVs, which were 4.29-fold higher in count than those released from vehicle-treated counterparts (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DAPT (10 μM) for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced PEVs release (by 45.55%).
source: Interestingly, pre-treatment of platelets with either DAPT (10 μM) or DBZ (10 µM), specific γ-secretase inhibitors, for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced PEVs release (by 45.55% and 41.98%, respectively) (Figure 3H), thus underscoring critical role of γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Pre-treatment of platelets with DBZ (10 µM) for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced PEVs release (by 41.98%).
source: Interestingly, pre-treatment of platelets with either DAPT (10 μM) or DBZ (10 µM), specific γ-secretase inhibitors, for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced PEVs release (by 45.55% and 41.98%, respectively) (Figure 3H), thus underscoring critical role of γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: γ-secretase activity plays a critical role in DLL-4-induced PEVs release.
source: Interestingly, pre-treatment of platelets with either DAPT (10 μM) or DBZ (10 µM), specific γ-secretase inhibitors, for 10 min led to significant drop in DLL-4-induced PEVs release (by 45.55% and 41.98%, respectively) (Figure 3H), thus underscoring critical role of γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduction in PEVs with γ-secretase inhibitors.

claim: Platelet activation is associated with phosphorylation of multiple cytosolic proteins on tyrosine residues.
source: Platelet activation is associated with phosphorylation of multiple cytosolic proteins on tyrosine residues (Golden et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Golden et al., 1990.

claim: Platelets treated with DLL-4 but not DLL-1 evoked increased tyrosine phosphorylation of peptides having Mr 72, 95, 110, and 124 kDa.
source: Platelets treated with DLL-4 but not DLL-1 evoked increased tyrosine phosphorylation of peptides having Mr 72, 95, 110, and 124 kDa, which was remarkably reduced in presence of DAPT and DBZ.
